description: AppSec Village at DEF CON 27 covers application security practices, testing strategies, and vulnerability detection. The talks explore CI/CD security, purple team strategies, cryptographic failures, hidden vulnerabilities, and the history of application security.

talks.title: Automate Pen Testing in Dockerized CI CD Environment
talks.teaser: Automate Pen Testing in Dockerized CI CD Environment
talks.summary:
### Integrating Automated Penetration Testing into CI/CD
At 00:00, Yanyan Wang presents an engineering framework for automating application penetration testing within containerized continuous integration and deployment (CI/CD) pipelines at the AppSec Village.

### Overcoming the Bottleneck of Manual Security Assessments
At 07:30, Wang discusses the disconnect between rapid DevOps deployment cycles and traditional periodic penetration testing. Relying solely on manual annual assessments leaves applications exposed, requiring security teams to shift dynamic testing left into automated delivery pipelines.

### Containerizing Dynamic Security Scanners
At 14:46, the presentation details packaging security tooling using Docker. Wang demonstrates how containerizing headless browser automation drivers, custom scanning scripts, and interception proxies creates reproducible testing environments that execute seamlessly across Jenkins and GitLab CI runners.

### Driving Security Scans via Automated Functional Tests
At 22:11, Wang explains how to achieve thorough application test coverage. By configuring existing Selenium and Cypress regression suites to proxy traffic through automated security engines like OWASP ZAP, the security scanner exercises authenticated application workflows without requiring manual crawling.

### Threshold Gates and Vulnerability Triage
Concluding between 31:52 and 43:27, Wang reviews pipeline policy enforcement. She outlines strategies for establishing severity thresholds, automatically filing bug tickets, and failing automated builds only on verified high-severity vulnerabilities to prevent developer fatigue.

talks.title: Keynote The Unabridged History of Application Security
talks.teaser: Keynote The Unabridged History of Application Security
talks.summary:
### Three Decades of Application Security Evolution
At 00:00, veteran application security educator Jim Manico delivers the inaugural keynote for the DEF CON 27 AppSec Village, chronicling thirty years of web application vulnerabilities, defensive frameworks, and cryptographic standards.

### The History of Web Encryption and Certificate Auditing
At 11:02, Manico traces the development of transport layer security from early Netscape SSL protocols to modern TLS 1.3. He highlights the 2009 launch of Qualys SSL Labs as a transformative milestone that automated cipher suite evaluation and forced enterprise web servers to eliminate legacy insecure configurations.

### Open-Source Foundations: OWASP, ModSecurity, and ZAP
At 22:02, the speaker explores the rise of open-source defensive initiatives. He reviews the 2001 founding of OWASP, the impact of the OWASP Top 10 awareness standard, the integration of the ModSecurity Core Rule Set into web application firewalls, and the maturation of Zed Attack Proxy (ZAP) into a professional auditing platform.

### Moving Beyond the "Pen Test and Pray" Paradigm
At 33:02 and 44:00, Manico critiques reactive security testing. Traditional models that rely solely on annual penetration tests fail to secure modern continuous deployment pipelines. He illustrates how modern application frameworks (such as React, Angular, and Spring) fundamentally hardened security by implementing context-aware output encoding and parameterized queries by default.

### Empowering Developers as Primary Defenders
Concluding at 55:02, Manico delivers an impassioned appeal for developer education. Organizations must move beyond blaming software developers for bugs; sustainable security requires investing in continuous secure coding training and embedding automated guardrails directly into developer IDEs and CI/CD pipelines.

talks.title: Vulnerabilities that Hide from Your Tools
talks.teaser: Vulnerabilities that Hide from Your Tools
talks.summary:
### Flaws That Escape Automated Security Scanners
At 00:00, application security educator Jillian Ratliff explores business logic flaws and architectural vulnerabilities that routinely bypass automated static (SAST) and dynamic (DAST) scanners at the AppSec Village.

### Strengths and Scope of Automated Tooling
At 05:55, Ratliff reviews what automated scanning tools do well. Rule-based tools excel at detecting predictable, syntax-level issues such as missing security headers, default passwords, outdated dependencies, and simple cross-site scripting patterns.

### The Blind Spots of Automated Analysis
At 11:46, the presentation examines why scanners produce false negatives. Automated tools lack contextual understanding of business requirements, struggling with non-English naming conventions, multi-factor authorization logic, and credentials stored in auxiliary documentation files.

### Business Logic Flaws and Parameter Tampering
At 17:43, Ratliff illustrates high-impact business logic vulnerabilities, including Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR), parameter manipulation in shopping carts, and race conditions during account transfers, demonstrating that scanners cannot determine whether an authorized action violates business policy.

### Cultivating Developer Security Mindsets
Concluding between 23:59 and 31:48, Ratliff advocates for interactive, continuous developer education. Rather than relying on annual compliance training, she encourages security teams to host monthly threat modeling sessions that empower developers to spot architectural flaws during code design.

talks.title: Welcome and Introductions
talks.summary:
### Launching the Inaugural AppSec Village
At 00:00, Erez Yalon takes the podium to open the first-ever AppSec Village at DEF CON 27, welcoming software engineers, penetration testers, and security researchers to a dedicated community space focused on application layer security.

### Community Origins and Volunteer Recognition
At 01:00, Yalon acknowledges the core organizing committee and volunteer staff, commending their months of grassroots effort in designing village infrastructure, curating technical presentations, and constructing interactive security labs.

### Bridging the Gap Between Builders and Breakers
The introductory remarks articulate the core mission of the AppSec Village: dismantling historical barriers between offensive hackers and software developers. The village emphasizes collaborative defense, secure architectural design, and practical software engineering.

### Overview of Village Tracks and Practical Labs
Concluding the opening address, Yalon previews the weekend's interactive programming, including threat modeling workshops, secure code review tournaments, and live secure development demonstrations, before introducing the opening keynote speaker.
